[THOUGHT]  
The summary states the patient is “unable to report on pain (intensity, quality, or temporal pattern)”, but it does *not* state whether the patient *lacks sensation*, *has neuropathy*, or is *asymptomatic*. “Unable to report” could reflect aphasia, dementia, delirium, language barrier, sedation, or other communication deficits — not necessarily peripheral sensory neuropathy. Therefore, inferring neuropathy from this statement is unsupported and was correctly flagged as UNDETERMINED.

All other findings must be interpreted strictly as written:  
- The wound is chronic (6 months), non-healing, and located on the right lower leg.  
- No signs of local infection or malignancy are *observed or reported*, but the note explicitly adds “though formal inspection findings were not documented” — meaning absence of erythema/warmth/etc. is *not confirmed*, only that they were not recorded. So those features are *unknown*, not absent.  
- Physical exam details (size, depth, margins, base, exudate, periwound skin) are *not specified* — i.e., entirely missing.  
- Dermoscopy was performed but yielded *no interpretive findings reported* — i.e., result is unknown.  
- Biopsy was obtained but results are *pending or unreported* — i.e., histopathology is unknown.  
- Lab data: CBC normal; wound culture negative. That is all that is known.  
- All other investigations (glucose, HbA1c, CMP, CRP, ABI, etc.) are explicitly listed as *not reported* — i.e., absent from the record.  

Thus, the only *confirmed, objective, and unambiguous findings* are:  
→ Chronic (6-month) non-healing wound on right lower leg  
→ Normal CBC  
→ Negative wound culture (aerobic/anaerobic/fungal)  
→ No documented signs of local infection or malignancy *— but with the critical qualifier that formal inspection was not documented*, so this is not evidence of absence.  

Given this extreme paucity of objective data, *no diagnosis in the differential can be supported over another on current evidence*. However, diagnostic reasoning requires identifying the *single most likely diagnosis* given what *is* known — and the only universally shared feature across all ulcers is *chronicity + location*. But location alone (“lower leg”) is non-specific: venous ulcers favor medial malleolus; arterial ulcers favor distal toes/heel; neuropathic ulcers favor weight-bearing areas (e.g., plantar forefoot) — yet *the exact anatomic site within the lower leg is not specified*.  

Crucially, the differential includes six possibilities — but one stands out as *most commonly associated with a 6-month non-healing lower leg wound in the absence of active infection or systemic inflammation*: **chronic venous stasis ulcer**. Why?  
- It is the *most prevalent type of chronic leg ulcer* in adults (70–90% of cases).  
- It frequently presents on the *gaiter area* (distal lower leg/ankle), matches the described location.  
- It often lacks prominent pain (though not always), and pain reporting status is indeterminate — so this neither supports nor refutes it.  
- It typically persists for months to years without intervention.  
- It is *not ruled out* by any test performed: normal CBC and negative culture are expected in uncomplicated venous ulcers.  
- In contrast:  
  • Arterial ulcers usually cause rest pain or tissue loss (gangrene) — not mentioned, but also *not assessed* (no ABI, no pulse exam).  
  • Neuropathic ulcers almost always occur in *diabetic or neurologic patients* — but diabetes is *not confirmed* (no glucose/HbA1c), and neurologic exam is *not documented*.  
  • Marjolin’s ulcer requires histologic proof — pending.  
  • Pyoderma gangrenosum is rare, typically *painful* and progressive — but pain status is unknown, and progression is not described.  
  • Atypical infections (e.g., mycobacterial) are possible but require specific testing — not done.  

So while *no diagnosis is confirmed*, **chronic venous stasis ulcer** is the *epidemiologically dominant, clinically typical, and least contradicted* diagnosis given the minimal confirmed data — and is therefore the single most likely diagnosis at this stage.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Non-healing wound on right lower leg, present for 6 months.  
- Complete blood count (CBC) with differential is within normal limits.  
- Wound culture (aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal) showed no growth of pathogenic organisms.  
- Chronic venous stasis ulcer is listed in the differential diagnosis as a leading consideration.  

[GAPS]  
- Formal wound description (location within lower leg, size, depth, margins, base, exudate, periwound skin changes) — not specified.  
- Ankle-brachial index (ABI) or Doppler ultrasound — not reported.  
- Fasting blood glucose and HbA1c — not reported.  
- Histopathology results — pending or unreported.  
- Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) and comprehensive metabolic panel — not reported.  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Chronic venous stasis ulcer
